World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Legendary Manchester United manager Alex Ferguson taken to hospital
World.content:
Legendary Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson has been taken to hospital after feeling unwell ahead of his former club's Premier League match against Liverpool.

The 84-year-old had been at Old Trafford for the match, which was played on Monday morning (AEDT).

Sky Sports reported Ferguson was conscious and had precautionary checks before being whisked away.

A United spokesperson said the club was unable to comment on Ferguson's status.

United coach Michael Carrick could not offer any updates after the match, which his team won 3-2.

"I did hear about it before the game," Carrick said.

"I was very affected by it, the news.

"I just don't know the latest, but we hope for him to be in good shape and we wish him all the best and certainly hope the result, when he hears about it, can give him a good boost."

Ferguson, who managed United from 1986 until his retirement in 2013, won 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League trophies during a glittering 26-year spell at the club.

He hoisted a total of 38 trophies with United.

Ferguson is a regular at the club's home matches and has a row of seats in the Old Trafford directors' box.

Reuters

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: How people power is helping to restore bus routes across Sydney
World.content:
Communities fighting to have their local bus or ferry routes restored should campaign hard and "stick it out for the long term", according to residents in the inner Sydney suburb of Pyrmont.

Lesley Bentley from the Pyrmont Peninsula Public Transport Forum (PPPTF) said her team of volunteers campaigned for three years to have the Me-Mel Ferry service returned to Pyrmont Wharf after it was axed in 2021 by the previous state government.

The PPPTF is now lobbying to have a new, permanent, CBD bus stop for the 389 service established on York Street, after its original stop on King Street was removed to make way for a cycleway.

Members of the Pyrmont Peninsula Public Transport Forum campaigned for three years. (ABC News: Jessica Kidd)

"You have to have a sustainable campaign, it has to be professional, and you have to be prepared to stick it out for the long term," Ms Bentley said.

"Getting the ferry back took three years, and we're hoping now, after four years, that we get a bus at 32 York Street."

It is a case study in local people power being played out in different communities across Sydney.

North-west bus service to run 24 hours a day

The NSW government has announced it is restoring the old M52 metro bus service between Parramatta and the CBD via Ryde, after the route was axed in 2021 by the former Liberal-National state government.

The new Route 52 will run 24 hours a day, seven days a week, connecting commuters across Sydney's north-west to the city via Victoria Road.

Route 52 will run 24 hours a day, seven days a week. (ABC News: Jessica Kidd)

It will commence services from June 21 and will be operated by 13 high-capacity "bendy" articulated buses.

Ryde Councillor Lyndal Howison said it was the result of a five-year campaign by local residents that was backed by local, state and federal MPs.

"It's definitely a case study in community advocacy," she said.

"People get really connected to their bus routes and especially one like this that is really, really well-used, so they were enraged when it was cut by the previous government."

Federal MP for Bennelong, Jerome Laxale, said restoring the key bus route was one of the major concerns raised by his constituents.

"To have this reliable, frequent, direct connection along Victoria Road is a no-brainer," he said.

"It's a lesson in democracy, right? You organise, come together, contact your local officials and sometimes it works."

Budget commitment to public transport

The restored Route 52 is part of a broader $452 million commitment in the NSW budget to create new bus routes, extend others and reinstate axed routes.

John Graham says the government is investing in buses. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

NSW Transport Minister John Graham said the funding would also be used to purchase an additional 50 new articulated or "bendy buses" which would go into service in parts of Ryde, Epping, Lane Cove, the eastern suburbs and northern beaches.

"We're investing in buses for the first time in a long time," he said.

"We've got more than 1,300 services back, we're continuing to invest, and also we're filling the driver shortage — we were left with more than 500 drivers short. That number is now down under 180 — that's a big investment in reliable bus services."

In response to the numerous grassroots campaigns across Sydney to get local bus services restored, Mr Graham indicated the government was listening.

"We're looking right across the network — matching buses to where people need them," he said.

"We've seen services come back here in Ryde, linking Parramatta and the CBD, also in the eastern suburbs, some services back. We're looking particularly at the northern beaches and the bus reliability challenges there."

Peter Gretch from the Rail, Tram and Bus Union said he welcomed any effort to restore bus services, but he said the only way to permanently improve service reliability and driver recruitment was for the NSW government to end all private bus contracts and bring services back into public ownership.

"I would hope for the sake of the travelling public, for the sake of the workers in this industry that [the government] get on their bike and start this process … and get buses back on track to what they should be," he said.

World.title: Former bosses to face court over fatal mine collapse
World.content:
Two former bosses at a central Queensland mine will face court this month on charges following the death of a worker and the serious injury of another in an underground mine collapse.

Graham Ronald Dawson, 62, and Henare Morgan, who was aged 25 at the time, were carrying out roof support works in a tunnel at the Crinum underground coal mine on September 14 when the rock around them collapsed and crushed the pair.

Mr Dawson was killed, while Mr Morgan was trapped next to his colleague's body for hours before being rescued and flown to the hospital with crush injuries to his upper legs.

Mine changed support method

The mine's operator and employer, Mastermyne Crinum Operations, was investigated and charged by the Queensland Work Health and Safety Prosecutor in 2024, along with underground mine manager David Sykes and site senior executive Steven Livingstone-Blevins.

Graham Dawson, 62, was killed at the Crinum underground mine in a roof collapse on September 14, 2021. (Supplied: Dawson family)

The prosecutor alleges Mr Sykes made changes to the methods workers used to support the mine drift, and they were signed off by Mr Livingstone-Blevins four days before the collapse.

Court documents allege shotcrete, effectively sprayed concrete, was used without the combined use of support beams known as steel sets.

It is alleged that Mr Livingstone-Blevins failed to identify the risks of abandoning the original method of strata support, which had been recommended by specialist expert advice, and he did not implement suitable controls to reduce the risk.

The prosecutor alleges Mr Sykes, through work and activities under his control, exposed workers to an unacceptable level of risk.

The pair was charged with two counts each of failure to discharge a health and safety obligation causing death or grievous bodily harm under the Coal Mining Safety and Health Act 1999.

Mastermyne Crinum Operations was also charged with one count of failing to discharge a health and safety obligation causing death grievous bodily harm, which remains outstanding.

The matters are due to be heard in the Emerald Magistrates Court later this month.

No parties have had to enter pleas at this stage.

Both Mr Livingstone-Blevins and Mr Sykes no longer work at Crinum underground mine or for any Mastermyne companies.

Mastermyne to appeal $7m fine

Mastermyne Crinum Operations has been fined $7 million over the death of Graham Dawson. (ABC Tropical North: Yasmine Wright Gittin)

Mastermyne Crinum Operations was fined $7 million in the District Court of Brisbane on May 1 after a jury found the company guilty of industrial manslaughter over the death of Mr Dawson.

It was Queensland's first recorded court sentence of industrial manslaughter.

However, company representatives filed an appeal immediately after it was handed down.

Graham Dawson, pictured with his two daughters, Katrina Edwards and Leesh Dawson. (Supplied: Dawson family)

Mr Dawson's daughters Katrina Edwards and Leesh Dawson delivered victim impact statements to the court, describing him as a beloved "Poppy" and close father, whose life had been cut short painfully.

Speaking outside court, Ms Dawson said no amount of money would bring her father back and the most important thing "was best practice is always followed and no more miners die".

"This was entirely preventable; there were numerous reports and evidence to show that," she said.

"The only thing that is going to bring any type of justice is to make sure laws are strengthened and that companies learn from this so that no-one else loses their life at work."

Mining and Energy Union general vice-president Stephen Smyth said he welcomed the charges.

"Workplace incidents leave a lifelong impact on affected workers, and it is vital that they are taken seriously by authorities," he said.

World.title: SA's history preservation organisation faces questions over future
World.content:
The future and finances of the National Trust of South Australia (NTSA) are being questioned amid disagreements with its volunteers.

The NTSA is a not-for-profit organisation, which conserves, manages and promotes more than 100 heritage sites across the state, mostly through volunteer-run branches.

One of these is based at Moonta, on the state's Yorke Peninsula, which is home to the 19th-century Cornish Mines.

The Moonta Branch Committee said they were "in shock" after NTSA stood them down and locked them out of properties they have passionately cared for for many years in February.

It is now suing the NTSA in the Supreme Court, and it wants the head office's decision to be overturned and the local committee reinstated.

Volunteers said they also wanted a parliamentary inquiry into the trust to examine its governance and financial sustainability.

While the organisation's chief executive conceded it currently only has "about two years" worth of cash reserves left, she said an inquiry would be a "wasteful" use of taxpayer money.

'No natural justice' in dismissal

The Moonta Mines Heritage Precinct has more than 100 volunteers working to preserve the town's historic mine sites, which are drawcards for tourists.

Moonta National Trust volunteers Robyn Knight and Sharron Ward are part of a group that's suing the charity in the Supreme Court. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

Former branch chair Sharron Ward said volunteers and committee members were left devastated by the head office's decision after the February meeting.

"As we were leaving, we could see the locksmiths changing the locks [on properties] and were basically just in shock," she said.

" One of us had been in the National Trust for 30 years and he described it as, 'the saddest day in his life'. "

After the meeting, NTSA circulated a media release announcing the Mines would be closed until Easter, as it was placing an "unreasonable burden" on volunteers.

Ms Ward said the committee had been left in the dark about the reasons behind their dismissal and argued there was "no natural justice or right of reply".

"The CEO said the reasons were confidential," she said.

" There were two members of the [NTSA Council] there and they said, 'It was a unanimous decision'. No more information was provided. "

NTSA chief executive Nicolette Di Lernia said the committee should have been aware of the issues through correspondence and meetings held in the several months prior.

National Trust SA chief executive Nicolette Di Lernia is based at Ayers House in Adelaide. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

She said money was not being budgeted for essential repairs and the branch was spending beyond its means.

The Moonta committee disputes this.

"Because the behaviour was not being addressed, and was in fact escalating, the [NTSA] council decided the level of risk it presented to the entire organisation was unacceptable," Ms Di Lernia said.

The Moonta Mines tourist railway and most other attractions remain closed. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

More regional unrest

Meanwhile, Renmark National Trust chair Ann Ryan said she also felt at odds with NTSA.

She said she felt powerless around the ownership of local assets after a parcel of land was sold in 2017 with the Renmark branch left with $460,000 of revenue.

Ms Ryan said those funds had been held by NTSA's head office and had largely not been returned, with only around $30,000 of interest received.

She said after wanting to re-invest the money with a bank that offered better returns, she was told it had not been kept separate from the organisation's pool of funds.

Renmark National Trust chair Ann Ryan has found herself questioning her NTSA membership. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

"At the last meeting we had with head office, we were just told, 'We don't have it'."

Ms Ryan said she now questioned whether it is worth being part of the trust at all.

"We've had to do what we've done here for 70 years without any input from them with finances," she said.

" They just don't understand we have a feeling of ownership. [As] a volunteer, it just grates you hearing, 'It's ours, it's ours'. "

Trust admits to challenges

Chief executive Nicolette Di Lernia acknowledged the connection communities have with local heritage, but said the trust's assets are held by the NTSA Council and not individual branches.

"There is a sense of ownership that they have established over time, that might be very real in their own minds, but that is not a reality," she said.

Excavation of the Moonta Mines began in the mid-19th century and it was at one stage the largest exporter of copper in the British Empire. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

Ms Di Lernia also acknowledged the organisation was "asset-rich" but struggling with cash flow after recording a more than $300,000 deficit last financial year.

"If we don't change how we operate — and we are a business as well as a charity — we have about two years until we reach the end of our reserves," she said.

Ms Di Lernia said to increase cash flow, the organisation would "from time to time sell off assets" and is "actively working" to sell some non-core assets.

She said they would accept prices below market value with the aim they remain open to the public.

Trust 'not fit for purpose'

Back at Moonta, the wider community had wrapped its arms around the local trust volunteers and the stood-down branch committee.

Around $5,000 had been donated to help fund the committee's legal action and more than 4,000 people had signed a petition calling for the reinstatement of the local committee.

Locals had also gotten involved to show their support, like Maggie Dawkins.

Moonta resident and retired public servant Maggie Dawkins has been helping the local branch with advice and letter-writing. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

Ms Dawkins is a retired public servant and has been gathering information and documentation around the operation of the NTSA.

She said she does not feel the National Trust Act adequately empowers local branch committees, instead favouring the state head office.

"Right now, the National Trust can do what they like because, legally, they can," she said.

"That doesn't make it right".

Ms Dawkins said a parliamentary inquiry should look at the rights of branches and examine the trust's financial sustainability.

Maggie Dawkins examines paperwork about the National Trust SA. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

Ms Di Lernia said it would be "wasteful" for taxpayers to foot the bill for an inquiry into a community organisation.

Recognition and reconciliation

The trust operates independently from government, but state environment minister Emily Bourke said she had asked the parties to "work together in good faith and resolve the situation amicably."

"The closure of the site not only affects those directly involved, but the local community in Moonta and surrounding areas, at a time when we need such fantastic tourist drawcards the most," she said.

The historic Moonta Sweet Shop was expected to reopen at Easter but remained closed. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

Ms Bourke declined to comment on her position of an inquiry.

Ms Di Lernia said the chance of reconciliation appeared difficult.

"They've now made it virtually impossible to be reinstated because they're just not working with us," she said.

"They've told us that they want to be autonomous, they don't want to be interfered with — that's not the organisation that they have volunteered with, they've volunteered with the National Trust."

The Moonta Sweet Shop is usually a stop for travellers who visit the town. (Supplied: Moonta National Trust)

For committee member Robyn Knight, it was not just about the reinstatement, but also a lack of recognition of volunteer efforts.

"The National Trust's approach has been 'You will do what you're told and that is it'," she said.

" That is not the way you should treat a person donating hours and hours of their time. "

A directions hearing for the Supreme Court case is set for May 29.

World.title: A region promised a hospital by 2028 watches as cows graze on the site
World.content:
Residents in one of Victoria's fastest-growing regions fear the state government will fail to deliver a new hospital on time, despite promising it four years ago.

In 2022, then-premier Daniel Andrews promised $675 million to build a new 223-bed hospital in West Gippsland at a greenfield site in Drouin by 2028.

But construction is yet to begin, four years after the announcement.

At the site, a herd of cows can be spotted grazing.

The existing West Gippsland Hospital in Warragul is 87 years old, and residents say it has reached the end of its life and the community has outgrown it.

The government allocated funding for planning and design in the 2023-24 budget, along with six other hospitals as part of a $320 million fund.

About 68,000 people live in the Baw Baw Shire, which covers Drouin and Warragul, and the council says that number is forecast to grow to almost 94,000 by 2046.

Community disappointment

Living with a heart condition, Drouin's Kaye Williams is no stranger to the healthcare system.

She has lived with her family in Drouin for more than 20 years and has used the West Gippsland Hospital multiple times over the past two decades.

Her most recent stay was a 10-day stint at the Warragul-based hospital, where she saw staff run off their feet.

"The hospital was at maximum capacity, and staff were literally running; you could see they were overworked," Ms Williams said.

"I was speaking to others who were waiting; they had come from Pakenham and Traralgon."

Drouin resident Kaye Williams lives with a chronic condition, and has used the West Gippsland hospital many times during her two decades living in the region.

Ms Williams said while she still hoped the hospital would be built in the coming years, she was worried she would not live long enough to see it.

"The hospital is a big problem. For these young families coming here, they're happy to have a new home and be out of the city; they expect facilities like a hospital," she said.

Hospital coming, minister says

Recently appointed Victorian Health Minister Harriet Shing said she had "long campaigned for and championed" the new West Gippsland hospital.

"We know that this is a growing part of the world and that the nurses, the midwives, the specialist workforce, and of course the entire workforce across that health service provide just the most extraordinary levels of care," said Ms Shing, whose electorate covers West Gippsland.

Harriet Shing has taken on new portfolios under the cabinet reshuffle. (ABC News)

Ms Shing said $65 million in funding had been allocated to both Wonthaggi and West Gippsland for upgrades, "to support their operations".

The ABC understands the funding will be used for roof repairs at the existing hospital in Warragul, with some used at a nearby aged care centre.

"There has been further work undertaken around the planning for that hospital, and of course, we will continue to invest in it, but that has been a priority of mine ever since before I was elected back in 2014," Ms Shing said.

"So we will continue to work to deliver that hospital."

Harsh realities

The current facility, constructed in Warragul in 1939 and extended multiple times since, is no longer fit for purpose.

Lifts are too small to carry essential equipment, paint peels off the walls in some rooms and there has been water damage from leaks and busted pipes.

In a statement, a hospital spokesperson acknowledged Ms Williams's concerns and that rising demand was putting the hospital under pressure.

"A new, purpose-built facility would significantly enhance our ability to meet current and future demand, improve patient flow, support more contemporary models of care, and provide a better experience for patients, their families and carers and our employees," the spokesperson said.

Baw Baw Shire Council Mayor Kate Wilson said the new hospital was "badly needed".

"Thirty-seven per cent of people in our shire also live with one or more long-term health conditions, compared to 31.4 per cent for Victoria," Ms Wilson said.

Liberal MP Wayne Farnham, who represents the community, said he regularly heard stories from community members of long wait times and a lack of resources at the hospital.

He said it was time the state government was honest about what stage plans for the hospital were at.

"The reality is the hospital will not be delivered by 2028. If they haven't finished the plans yet, it's still going to take four or five years to build the hospital," he said.

Wayne Farnham says the public needs to be updated on the status of plans for the promised West Gippsland hospital. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Spencer)

"But what the government has to do is actually provide the community with an update of actually what's going on. Have they finished the plans? Is it getting ready for tender?

"At least that gives the community some hope that it's actually going to be delivered. But unfortunately, we're not getting that transparency from the government."

World.title: Australia's most remote communities losing essential services due to price of fuel
World.content:
If you thought fuel prices were high in the capital cities, residents in some of Australia's most remote communities are still paying up to $4 for a litre of diesel.

Yindjibarndi woman Rachel Samson, who lives in Roebourne, 1,500 kilometres north of Perth, said she has had to drastically reduce her driving.

"If I don't have enough fuel for the car, I walk to work," she said.

The war in the Middle East has sent fuel costs skyrocketing, and while federal government intervention has seen prices drop in the nation's capital cities, there has been little relief in remote towns.

Rachel Samson says $100 is no longer enough to fill her tank. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

The price of fuel in Roebourne remains around $3 per litre, and Ms Samson said it was stopping community members participating in important cultural events, like sorry business, which often involves driving hundreds of kilometres.

"If there was sorry business in Onslow, I wouldn't take my car — I don't think it would make it that far," she said.

"It chews up a lot of petrol and it's just too much."

She said people would continue to struggle if the prices do not go down soon.

Nyikina woman Pat Riley says residents in her community were forced to miss out on important events due to high fuel costs. (ABC News: Michael Atkin)

Further north of Roebourne, at Pandanus Park Community, diesel is $4 a litre and chairperson Patricia Riley said people were also being forced to miss funerals and other significant events.

"It affected us a lot, especially as a remote mob, because a lot of us still practice our culture," she said.

" We don't have the dollars to fill our car up with a full tank to go to another community and then come back. "

Food prices higher

In the Western Desert community of Kunawarritji, the cost of a recent food delivery truck, which had to drive 17 hours, cost an additional $5,000 due to fuel price rises.

Fewer tourists are passing through the Kunawarritji community and buying from the store. (Supplied: Jarni Blakkarly)

But the reduction of tourists along the popular Canning Stock Route, which spans 2,000 kilometres in northern WA, has meant less people are buying from the community's store.

"The fuel price has gone up, so the store has to recover the costs from the transport, so it's a bit of an issue there," Kunawarritji CEO Chris Flood said.

"Tourism is a major part of Kunuaraitji and you only have it a few months of the year."

Jobs on the line

Fuel is also impacting the future employment of Martu people in Kunawarritji and other remote East Pilbara communities.

Non-for-profit organisation Kanyirninpa Jukurrpa (KJ) general manager Tim Schneider said 500 Martu people were employed through the ranger program, but fuel prices were threatening its viability.

Tim Schneider says ranger programs offer essential incomes for Martu people. (Supplied: Tim Schneider )

"If we have to slow down the program significantly, then Martu employment will drop … and people won't have the money in their pocket to buy the essential items," he said.

There could also be"serious ramifications" for the next fire season if rangers can not burn parts of the 13.6 million hectares of land they look after, he said.

Legal services wound back

Meanwhile, Aboriginal Family Legal Services CEO Corina Martin said workers had been asked to limit their travel to communities that could be reached using a single tank of fuel.

The not-for-profit organisation delivers outreach services to remote communities across WA, providing legal support and community education.

Remote communities vulnerable to global fuel crisis Remote communities' reliance on diesel fuel for power leaves them vulnerable in a global crisis.

Ms Martin said the fuel crisis had already led to increased isolation and financial pressures and would have a "profound impact" on remote communities if it continued.

"For the clients out in these regions, if they are going through domestic violence, it reduces the ability for them to leave the community or escape," she said.

Back in Kunawarritji, Mr Schneider said remote communities were often "out of mind and out of sight", and said he hoped the government would support organisations delivering essential services to communities.

"They're some of the most vulnerable people in these communities," he said.

World.title: Tenants having to fight to fix unlivable, unsafe, unhealthy public housing
World.content:
Dana Wing just wants her family to live in a house that doesn't risk making them sick.

For the past six months, they have been unable to safely use their shower in their Homes Tasmania public housing property due to mould inundation behind the walls.

It's spread to other parts of the house — and there's nothing the family with four children can do about it.

"It makes it hard to try to have baths in the morning of school, especially coming into winter and the colder weather," Ms Wing said.

She notified Homes Tasmania in September last year. Reports were done, insurance staff visited, and the mould was characterised as category two, meaning substantial repairs must be done.

Dana Wing says she's "got nowhere" in trying to get the problem fixed over the past eight months. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Silicone was replaced, only for the mould to come through again.

As the months tick by, Ms Wing says she has no answers, and an offer of a different house was deemed unsuitable for her children.

They are only using the bath, which adds to the stress, while Ms Wing has advice from her doctor to avoid the mould to prevent exacerbating her asthma.

"I've basically got nowhere in the last eight months," she said.

"I understand Homes Tasmania has got a lot of houses out there, and a lot of people to take care of, I understand there's a waiting list.

" Just because it's not visible doesn't mean it doesn't have a side effect on our health. "

The mould behind the walls has spread to other parts of the house, requiring extensive rectification works that are yet to be confirmed. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

A Homes Tasmania spokesperson said delays can occur to significant remediation works if there is no alternative property to relocate tenants.

"When there is an insurance claim involved, this needs to be reviewed and can also cause further delays," they said.

The Wing family are not the only ones in Tasmania who have had to wait for solutions from public and social housing providers.

Years for cockroach infestation solution

Case files for 2025 obtained by the ABC under right to information laws show a range of examples where residents are having to obtain orders from the regulator — the Residential Tenancy Commissioner (RTC) — to have critical housing issues rectified, taking months or even years.

One tenant moved into a public housing complex in mid-2021 and soon noticed a cockroach infestation, their case file shows.

"I called Homes Tas and was told it was up to me to get rid of them so buy some of the bombs for cockroaches … I did this several times and still do now," she wrote.

"I can't afford thousands for a fumigator … I shouldn't have to anyway."

The cockroaches ate through the wiring of the oven, which Homes Tasmania replaced, and then ate through the wiring of the second oven, which Homes Tasmania would not replace.

In addition to a cockroach infestation in the broader complex, the tenant says the property was in extremely poor condition when they moved in. (Supplied)

By late 2024, the residents had set up a makeshift kitchen outside under a tarp, running an extension cord through the window to power a portable stove top.

They had to take the matter to the regulator.

"The cockroach infestation is an issue throughout the whole complex … unless the whole area is fumigated, they will continue to be a problem," the application reads.

"Homes Tasmania continue to refer to their policy that the tenant is responsible for managing this."

The regulator treated it as urgent due to an oven being an essential service, but Homes Tasmania did not respond.

It was ordered to replace the oven and undertake pest control.

These repairs cost Homes Tasmania $2,700.

Tenant blamed for wet carpet caused by pavers

A Homes Tasmania tenant noticed that their lounge room carpet would become wet in heavy rain, a situation that continued for at least 15 months.

The problem persisted despite a minor fix to the roof, so the insurance provider was called in to inspect it.

The tenant was initially blamed for the water ingress, but a report showed it was due to the design of the property, causing further delays. (Supplied)

In its response to a formal complaint by the tenant, Homes Tasmania cited part of the insurer's report that appeared to blame the tenant:

"… the moisture in the carpet was likely caused by nearby plants or [the tenant's] puppy, rather than the roof leak, and subsequently closed the claim."

But the insurers' report had another possible reason, which Homes Tasmania did not mention at that time.

"The pavers outside the sliding door are at the same height as the main internal floor … water could be sponged up from outside and distributed via the slab if there is no damp proof course installed, causing dampness to the carpet via the internal slab.

"This should be investigated."

The tenant had repeatedly raised concerns about the pavers.

Do you know more? Contact Adam Holmes at holmes.adam@abc.net.au.

In ordering Homes Tasmania to fix the problem, the regulator noted that it had not been investigated despite the insurer's report.

"It is not reasonable the tenant should live with carpet described as damaged beyond restoration through no apparent fault of their own," they wrote.

Other repairs to the property were also not completed in time, for which Homes Tasmania "sincerely apologises".

It was also warned by the regulator that further failures to meet repair deadlines could result in compliance action against the state-run public housing provider.

Bathroom unusable

In another case — involving a social housing provider — a new skirting board was installed to conceal mould, rather than rectify it.

In response to the regulator, the provider promised that further repairs would be "guided by its contractor".

The ABC understands that the new repairs are yet to occur, and the tenant has been advised that a full reconstruction is required for the bathroom.

Despite more families sleeping in cars, they're not a priority for housing An analysis of 12 months of urgent housing and homelessness attendances in Tasmania has shown an alarming spike in people with dependent children needing help.

The matter has been ongoing for 15 months, during which time the tenant and their child have had limited access to their bathroom; they are waiting for appropriate relocation.

A social housing provider also did not respond to another tenant's concerns about the state of their back fence, which had resulted in children not being able to use the backyard due to fears of the neighbour's dog.

They also had to take the matter to the regulator, which ordered the provider to carry out repairs.

Regulator a last resort for tenants

These are just the matters that resulted in orders from the Residential Tenancy Commissioner, considered a last resort.

Alex Bomford, from the Tasmanian Tenants' Union, said public and social housing tenants were regularly raising concerns about delays in repairs to substandard housing.

Tasmanian Tenants' Union solicitor Alex Bomford says Homes Tasmania should be setting an example for all housing providers to aspire to, but that this isn't occurring. (ABC News)

Mould is the most common issue, along with pests, leaks and structural issues.

"Homes Tasmania should be a model landlord, so every other housing provider should aspire to reach their standards," Mr Bomford said.

" It shouldn't be the case that Homes Tasmania should be forced to carry out repairs that they're obviously required to do. "

He said there is a tendency in the public, social and private housing sectors to "blame the tenants" for problems in the first instance.

In regard to mould, Homes Tasmania advises tenants that cooking, having a shower, and "breathing" are contributing factors, and that they should open doors and windows to prevent it.

Loading...

Mr Bomford said public and social housing tenants had fewer options.

"If you leave your social housing property, you're back at the end of the list, and you don't have anywhere to go," he said.

Tasmania is the only state where there is no clear process for tenants to seek a rent reduction for when essential services are unavailable, or when parts of their property are uninhabitable.

The state's tenancy laws are currently being reviewed.

Housing stock continues to age

A review of Homes Tasmania, released last year, pointed to the ageing nature of the state's social and public housing as a worsening cost risk, and noted frustrations at property maintenance requests.

The average age of social and public housing in Tasmania is 38 years, and 37 per cent is more than 40 years old.

A new property maintenance contractor panel has been established to attempt to resolve public housing maintenance issues faster. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The government is now in the process of replacing Homes Tasmania after the review pointed out funding uncertainty and policy constraints.

A Homes Tasmania spokesperson said rectifying water damage and completely removing mould is a "complex and time-consuming task".

"If the cause of mould is identified as being due to structural issues or water leaks, Homes Tasmania takes appropriate action to fix any underlying problems," they said.

A new property maintenance contractor panel started in the state's south in July, and will be introduced in the north and north-west this year, in an effort to resolve maintenance issues faster.

World.title: What you need to know about Queensland's train station staffing changes
World.content:
Amid ongoing industrial action, another rift has emerged between unions and the Queensland Rail — this time over staffing at south-east Queensland stations.

From Tuesday, some stations will no longer be staffed past 1pm and will be unstaffed on weekends.

While Queensland Rail has defended its rostering, the state's main transport union claims the changes will make commuters less safe, with concerns also raised about the impact on people with disability.

So, what exactly is changing, and which stations will be impacted?

New rostering system

In short, Queensland Rail says it needs to rejig where it allocates staff to support stations experiencing a surge in patronage, as well as imminent additions to the network at Merrimac and Hope Island.

"Changes to our rosters are based on facts and patronage statistics which show that some stations require more staff at certain times, while others are not as busy," Queensland Rail SEQ Executive General Manager, Rob Hill, said.

Staffing is set to change at several stations across south-east Queensland. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

For example, there will be more station staff now at Dinmore Station during peak hours, while Buranda Station will be staffed only between 5am and 1pm, and will be unstaffed on weekends.

"Queensland Rail developed the rosters to ensure station attendance aligns with customer demand and operations, improving efficiencies and supporting job security for our workforce," Mr Hill said.

Which stations are being impacted?

According to data provided to the ABC by the Rail, Tram, and Bus Union (RTBU), roughly one third of south-east Queensland's 153 stations will no longer be staffed on weekends, while 19 won't be staffed after 1pm during the week (previously they were staffed until 7pm).

Queensland Rail declined a request from the ABC to verify all of the union's data, but did confirm rostering changes for a handful of stations.

Station Staffed hours prior to May 4 Changes from May 4 Roma Street First to last service, Mon to Sun No change Milton 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun Removing weekend shifts. Increased staffing during special events Toowong 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun Saturday 0800-1600

Removing the Sunday shift Booval 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat and Sun Removing weekend shifts Springfield 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun 0500 - 1300 weekdays Removing weekend shifts Deagon 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun 0500 - 1300 weekdays Removing weekend shifts Darra 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun Weekdays unchanged Modifying weekend shifts 0800 - 1600 Buranda 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun 0500 - 1300 weekdays Removing weekend shifts

Changes at some stations, like Toowong, are minimal while others, such as Springfield, are likely to have a more significant impact on commuters.

Queensland Rail told the ABC new staffing hours for all impacted stations will be available on its website from Tuesday.

What are opponents saying?

The RTBU has labelled the changes "extreme" and said they will make impacted stations less safe. They will also disadvantage commuters who rely on assistance to travel, including people with disabilities, elderly passengers and tourists, it said.

Peter Allen says the removal of station staff would have have consequences for basic human needs. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

"There is innumerable studies which talk about how having somebody at a station provides safety," RTBU Queensland State Secretary, Peter Allen, said.

"For people who might come along to engage in anti-social behaviour, they're less likely to do so if there's somebody at the station."

Mr Allen said the changes would also have consequences for basic human needs.

" No station staff means the toilet gets locked. So what happens when somebody needs to use the toilet? "

Advocates for people with disabilities are also sceptical.

Tim McCallum says the staffing changes would impact people with mobility devices. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Tim McCallum, Queensland performing artist and one of the state's most high-profile advocates, regularly takes the train from Springfield — one of the stations facing a six-hour reduction in staffing during the week.

He uses a wheelchair and requires assistance from a train guard or platform station master to board trains.

"[These changes don't just impact] people with mobility devices, it might be people with vision impairment, lots of other disabilities that station staff really assist the community with," Mr McCallum said.

He believed the changes put the onus on people with a disability to let stations know in advance if they were going to be travelling at an unstaffed hour.

" Why should the disability community have to work harder to access public transport like everybody else does? "

Will support be available during unstaffed periods?

Yes, but opponents do not believe they will offset the loss of on-station staff at the impacted train stations.

In addition to the rostering changes, Queensland Rail has doubled its ranks of specialist security officers from 35 to 70.

Some south-east Queensland train stations will now be unstaffed on weekends. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

The so-called 'Authorised Officers', who patrol both stations and trains, are trained in de-escalation and can issue infringement notices.

"[Authorised Officers] work in shifts, which include morning, evening and night times," Queensland Rail SEQ Executive General Manager, Rob Hill, said.

"There is 24-hour security monitoring of the train network through more than 12,000 CCTV cameras, Mobile Security Dog Teams ... and private security officers who conduct targeted patrols of our network."

There will also be a new 10-person mobile customer support team that can respond to incidents during network disruptions or during busy school periods.

Queensland Rail has introduced a new 10-person mobile customer support team. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

Mr Hill pointed out on-board train guards can lay ramps for passengers who need assistance to board when stations are unstaffed.

But Mr McCallum said this was not a "feasible" solution and would likely drag out the time trains are stopped at stations.

"The train guards, who do a fantastic job, [are] now expected to see a person with a disability down the end of the platform, walk all the way down to the middle of the platform, take a ramp out of the container, fold the ramp out and allow the person with mobility issues onto the train," he said.

"I think that's turning a one-minute job into a five-minute job ... which means trains are going to be delayed for anyone that requires mobility assistance," he said.

A Queensland Rail spokesperson told the ABC it was confident having on-board train guards provide mobility assistance would not impact its operations.

Is this related to the ongoing industrial action?

The rostering changes are not related to tomorrow's escalation in industrial action that will see 273 fewer train services running.

That dispute, around pay and conditions, is ongoing.

Unions launched industrial action over Easter, amid a pay dispute with Queensland Rail. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

Last week, the RTBU hinted at further rail disruptions after rejecting another pay offer from Queensland Rail.

But Mr Allen said the union is trying to reverse what he called the station "cuts".

"At the moment, we're negotiating six agreements simultaneously," he said.

"One of them ... covers people who are [employed] in stations. It's no surprise we are trying to negotiate an end to the cuts in stations using that process."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to travel to Italy this week to meet with Pope Leo, a Vatican source said, as President Donald Trump’s attacks against the Catholic pontiff have drawn criticism across the political spectrum.

The meeting, the first known in-person encounter between Leo and a US cabinet official in nearly a year, is expected to take place on Thursday, said a senior source familiar with the pope’s plans.

The pope emerged in recent weeks as an outspoken critic of the US-Israeli led war with Iran, after previously criticising the Trump administration’s hard-line anti-immigration policies.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance met with the Pope in 2025. Vatican Media via AP

Trump sharply criticised Leo on social media several times in April, at one point calling the pontiff “terrible”, in attacks that drew wide attention while Leo was on a four-nation Africa tour.

World.title: Suaalii’s dream Twickenham debut is a millstone around his neck
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionSuper Rugby Suaalii’s dream Twickenham debut is a millstone around his neck Paul Cully May 4, 2026 — 5:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii’s muted return against the Western Force in Sydney on Friday night was partly due to the visitors’ smart tactics of starving the Waratahs of the ball. It was further evidence of how adept Australian teams are at shutting each other down. Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii (centre) made a quiet return for the Waratahs against the Western Force on Friday night. Getty Images It was also because he missed more than a month of rugby due to a hamstring injury, and his timing isn’t quite in sync with his teammates. But the third part of this narrative is that the quality of Suaalii’s debut performance against England at the end of 2024 was inflated far above reality.



It has set an expectation that he will dominate every contest, and no other No.13 in the world is doing that. That Twickenham Test against England, won 42-37 by the Wallabies, has been like a millstone around his neck ever since, though it’s clear he is still very much in the learning stage of his rugby career. The Waratahs’ Lawson Creighton did a great job of negating Zac Lomax’s impact in the air. Getty Images But don’t be surprised if he is much more influential against the Highlanders in Dunedin next Saturday afternoon. The Force’s ability to limit Suaalii’s impact was mirrored by how cleverly the Waratahs limited Zac Lomax’s influence under the high ball and reflected a bigger picture: the four Australian teams have been each other’s worst enemies in Super Rugby. Look at the ladder: despite the Brumbies having a 4-1 record against the Kiwis and the Reds are 2-2 in trans-Tasman games ahead of their clash with the Chiefs on Friday, the Reds are fourth, the Brumbies are sixth, the Waratahs are eighth and the Force are 10th.



So, the Waratahs’ use of Lawson Creighton to contest the high ball against Lomax was just the latest sign of how adept Australian teams have become at negating each other. The Waratahs have beaten the Brumbies and Reds, while the Queenslanders have swept the Brumbies but lost at home to the Force – and on it goes. Equality is hurting Australia The supreme irony of the dilemma described above is that an equal distribution of talent – what should be a force for good – is actually hurting Australia’s hopes of securing a home play-off. Man for man, the Australian squads are relatively even compared to the situation in New Zealand, where the weakest side – the Highlanders – is a level below the other four. The other four Kiwi sides have beaten the Highlanders so far, and the Hurricanes and Chiefs are odds-on to defeat them twice before the end of the regular season. Advocates for a trans-Tasman player draft are on the right track but are overreaching.



Australia should tell New Zealand they need to replicate the talent spread present in their own system, where the form Australian No.9, No.10 and outside back are all in Perth (see item below). Failing that, Rugby Australia should push hard for a conference system in a 10-team competition next year, where the top two sides in Australia make the semi-finals. Super Rugby team of the week 1. Sef Fa’agaese (Force), 2. Brandon Paenga-Amosa (Force), 3. Zane Nonggorr (Reds), 4. Seru Uru (Reds), 5. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto (Reds), 6. Joe Brial (Reds), 7. Fraser McReight (Reds), 8. Nick Champion de Crespigny (Force), 9. Henry Robertson (Force), 10. Ben Donaldson (Force) - player of the week, 11. Dylan Pietsch (Force), 12. Hunter Paisami (Reds), 13. Josh Flook (Reds), 14. Filipo Daugunu (Reds), 15. Mac Grealy (Force) Good signs for Joe Schmidt The Reds-Brumbies game in Brisbane was the best match of the weekend. It was intense, but punctuated by moments of individual skill: Joe Brial’s pick up down the right-hand touchline and Jock Campbell’s big touch finder off his left boot among them.



As the July Tests approach, it was a reassuring sight for Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt. The Leinster contingent in first-up opponents Ireland again showed their quality over the weekend by beating Toulon to qualify for the Champions Cup final, so the Wallabies will need to hit the ground running. Big Lukhan Salakaia-Loto is in great form, Hunter Paisami was nice and direct, and the Reds’ back row of Brial, Fraser McReight and Harry Wilson pipped their opposites. The Robertson, Donaldson show Force No.10 Ben Donaldson is in career-best form, but it is almost impossible to separate his excellent performance against the Waratahs from the quality of his halves partner Henry Robertson. The Force No.9 will make his Wallabies debut this year – you can put your house on it. Related Article Waratahs ‘We were bullied’: Waratahs take a beating from Force in Sydney



No other halfback in Australia has linked his forwards and backs as well as Robertson during the past month or so, and his running threat around the ruck creates space for Donaldson. His box-kicking is also outstanding. As mentioned in item one, only the strength of Waratahs No.10 Creighton under the high ball in Sydney prevented Lomax from having a field day. But not even Creighton could stop Dylan Pietsch, the Force winger who is now setting the standard for Australian outside backs. Watch every match of Super Rugby Pacific live and exclusive on Stan Sport.

World.title: ASX set to slip, Wall Street sets more records
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip, Wall Street sets more records Stan Choe May 4, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market set more records after Apple, Estee Lauder and others joined the list of companies delivering fatter profits for the start of the year than analysts expected. Easing oil prices also helped steady the stock markets around the world that were still open on the May Day holiday. The S&P 500 climbed 0.3 per cent to its latest all-time high and closed out a fifth straight winning week. That’s its longest such streak since 2024. The Dow Jones dipped 152 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.9 per cent to its own record. Wall Street continues to rise despite the uncertainty of the Iran war. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures on Saturday pointing to a fall of 23 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.99¢ at 5.15am AEST. Front of mind for investors this week will be the Reserve Bank’s interest rates decision on Tuesday afternoon. Apple led the way on Wall Street after the iPhone seller reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Because it’s one of Wall Street’s biggest stocks in terms of overall size, Apple’s rally of 3.3 per cent was by far the strongest force lifting the S&P 500.



Stock prices generally follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, and US companies have been blowing past expectations for earnings in the first three months of 2026. That’s even with the war with Iran and high oil prices souring confidence for many US households. A little more than a quarter of the companies in the S&P 500 have reported already, and 84 per cent of them have topped analysts’ estimates, according to FactSet. The index is on track to deliver roughly 15 per cent growth in profit from a year earlier. Related Article Opinion

Cybersecurity The AI craze is a double-edged sword for our banking giants Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Estee Lauder’s stock climbed 3.4 per cent after reporting better earnings than expected, thanks in part to strength in China, and it raised some of its upcoming financial forecasts. Sandisk jumped 8.3 per cent after the maker of storage for computers blew past analysts’ expectations for profit thanks in part to voracious demand from data centres. Colgate-Palmolive added 2.2 per cent after likewise delivering bigger results than expected, though CEO Noel Wallace said it expects “volatile macroeconomic conditions and slower category growth to continue in 2026.”



The main uncertainty for the global economy is where oil prices are heading because of the Iran war. Oil prices spurted higher early this week on worries that the war will keep the Strait of Hormuz closed for a long time. That would in turn keep oil tankers pent up in the Persian Gulf instead of delivering crude to customers worldwide. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s war has been a gift to an industry he detests But such moves have been quick to reverse throughout the war, as hopes rise and fall for a reopening of the strait. On Friday, the price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 2 per cent to settle at $US108.17. Brent was selling for a little more than $US70 per barrel before the war began. That rise since the end of February helped the two biggest US oil companies report stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. But stock prices nevertheless fell for both Exxon Mobil, 1 per cent, and Chevron, 1.4 per cent, as oil prices regressed Friday and each reported drops in net income from a year earlier. All told, the S&P 500 rose 21.11 points to 7,230.12. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 152.87 to 49,499.27, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 222.13 to 25,114.44.



The fall in oil prices helped Treasury yields ease in the bond market. So did a report in the morning that said growth for US manufacturing was a touch softer last month than economists expected. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.38 per cent from 4.40 per cent late Thursday. Such dips can make mortgages and other loans for US households and businesses cheaper, and they also tend to give upward pushes to prices for stocks and all kinds of other investments. Many stock markets worldwide were closed for May Day. Among the indexes still trading, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.4 per cent, and London’s FTSE 100 slipped 0.1 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Antonelli wins Miami Grand Prix as Oscar Piastri finishes third
World.content:
Breaking SportFormula 1 Antonelli wins Miami Grand Prix as Oscar Piastri finishes third May 4, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami, Florida: Kimi Antonelli won the Miami Grand Prix on Sunday for his third consecutive Formula 1 victory as the 19-year-old Mercedes driver continued to show he’s a legitimate championship contender. Antonelli started from the pole but had a slick start on a damp surface at the Miami International Autodrome. Threats of heavy rain led F1 to move up the start of the race by three hours, and there was an early morning heavy thunderstorm with lightning strikes directly over the Hard Rock Stadium, but it had cleared by the time the event began. Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli of Italy celebrates after winning the Miami Formula One Grand Prix. AP Still, the first 25 laps were attacked by the drivers as if the rain could return at any moment, and it led to early chaos, even for Antonelli. Charles Leclerc of Ferrari had a spectacular start from third and surged to the lead when Antonelli went wide off course trying to defend. A split-second later, Max Verstappen spun trying to hold off Leclerc when the two cars made contact.



The contact caused Verstappen, who started a season-best second, to plummet to ninth after the spin. Antonelli recovered and reclaimed the lead on the fifth lap, and the leaders briefly swapped positions as Leclerc moved back to the front before reigning world champion Lando Norris took over on Lap 14. Oscar Piastri before the race. Getty Images Verstappen worked his way through the field and briefly took the lead as others pitted, but Antonelli beat Norris off pit lane and reclaimed the lead for good once everything cycled out. Norris finished second, 3.2 seconds behind Antonelli, as the Italian and teammate George Russell have won the first four races of this season for Mercedes. Leclerc was going to finish third until Oscar Piastri of McLaren passed him on the final lap. Leclerc spun and settled for sixth.



Russell was fourth and Verstappen finished a season-best fifth for Red Bull. Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari was seventh. Oscar Piastri overtook Charles Leclerc to finish third. Getty Images Cadillac, in its first race in the United States, had an unimpressive weekend on the track even as it splashed its way through Miami with appearances and events. Sergio Perez finished 16th and Valtteri Bottas was 18th — the last car to finish in the 22-driver field. Messy start Isack Hadjar had been disqualified after qualifying and started last, but his race lasted five laps before he drove his Red Bull into the wall. Hadjar was openly angry at the result as he pounded his helmet before climbing from his car and angrily stomping away.



Seconds later, Pierre Gasly and Liam Lawson made contact that caused Gasly’s car to do a full rollover. The Frenchman’s car ended stuck with its rear tires atop a barrier and he climbed from the half-suspended BMW on his own. Up next The Canadian Grand Prix is next for F1 at Circuit Gilles Villeneuve in Montreal on May 24. That date was traditionally held by the Monaco Grand Prix, but a tweak to the schedule shifted it to Canada, and F1 will no longer be the opener for what had traditionally been the most prolific day in motor sport. The F1 race typically opened the morning ahead of the Indianapolis 500 and then NASCAR’s Coca-Cola 600. Because the race is in Canada and not Monaco, it has a late afternoon start time and will follow the Indy 500 and end during the NASCAR race. World.title: Warnings over Russian ‘blood oil’ as Asian fuel imports increase
World.content:
BusinessMarketsBlood Oil Warnings over Russian ‘blood oil’ as Asian fuel imports increase Angus Delaney May 4, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s increased reliance on Asian fuel is putting the nation at risk of importing sanctioned Russian “blood oil” via third countries, experts and pro-Ukraine groups say, as the US-Israeli war on Iran threatens global energy supplies. The federal government has scrambled to shore up its oil supply after petrol prices surged and panic buying dried some service stations of fuel when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz. Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz some Asian nations – including the three countries the government recently reaffirmed its energy trade ties with – increasing their intake of Russia oil, raising concerns it could flow into Australia. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac The disruption to global energy supplies is the latest flashpoint in the domestic debate over Australia’s sanctions on Russian oil and the ethical considerations businesses face. “Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, there has been a significant supply shortage on oil globally, particularly in Asia,” said Vaibhav Raghunandan, an analyst at the Finland-based think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “Russian oil has stepped in to fill the gap.”



This includes Singapore, Brunei and Malaysia – the three countries the federal government recently reaffirmed its energy trade ties with, raising concerns Russian oil processed by these nations will find its way to Australia. Although direct oil imports from Russia are banned by Australia, domestic buyers can source it from a third country after it has undergone “substantial transformation” – such as being refined – under what critics call a loophole that funds the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine. Anthony Albanese this month touring Jurong Island, Singapore’s oil hub. Dominic Lorrimer Analysis of shipping and government data estimates by CREA, a philanthropy-funded independent research organisation focused on air pollution, found Australia has already sent $2.4 billion indirectly to Moscow via this loophole since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. This forms a small slice of the $1.6 trillion Russia has earned from all its fossil fuel sales over this period. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last month announced Australia had secured an extra 400 million litres of diesel, including from Brunei, Malaysia and South Korea. Ukrainian groups worry that Australia’s increase of fuel imports from, in particular, Brunei, which is a major importer of Russian crude, will undermine our support of Kyiv.



In the past 15 months, 3.2 million tonnes of oil products from Brunei’s Hengyi refinery – which relies heavily on Russian crude and is jointly owned with China – has been imported to Australia, CREA analysis found. Of this, 1.1 million tonnes was refined from Russian crude. Related Article Visual story

Blood Oil How Putin’s ‘ghost ships’ put billions worth of blood oil into Australian cars In March alone, seven shipments from Hengyi refinery were offloaded in Australia. Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organisations chair Kateryna Argyrou said Labor could not claim to stand with Ukraine while “allowing money to flow in the Kremlin’s coffers”. “While Australia has taken a strong position in support of Ukraine, it continues to import Russian-origin fuel products through a sanctions loophole that allows Russian crude refined in third countries to enter our supply chains,” said Argyrou.



“As the prime minister engages with partners in Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei to secure fuel supply, it is critical that Australia ensures we are not importing more fuel derived from Russian crude or oil products.” Argyrou said there was not only “a real risk that more Australian dollars will flow into the Russian war machine” but also through to Iran, the Kremlin’s closest ally in the Middle East. Raghunandan said the federal government should prioritise strengthening its trade ties with South Korea, a more ethical refiner that has not imported any Russian crude since May 2022. Albanese’s office referred questions to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. A spokesperson for the department said the government was focused on securing oil supply and supporting broader energy security with its key partners. “We don’t want to see Russia benefit from the conflict in the Middle East to fund its unjustified war against Ukraine,” the spokesperson said.



Ben Neville, a University of Melbourne associate professor in corporate sustainability, said businesses needed to seriously consider the ethical implications of buying fuel that contained Russian oil, even if it was not sanctioned. “As human beings, we should always be integrating ethics into our decision-making, and that includes when we are playing roles in organisations,” he said. “Just putting on a grey suit, and walking into a corporate headquarters doesn’t mean that suddenly you’re in a world that’s devoid of ethics.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Brunei with His Majesty Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah. AAP Neville said although there was a potential financial downside and that corporate sustainability was often falsely portrayed as “a left-wing woke ideology”, there was a strong business case, too. He pointed to BP’s decision to cut its interests in Russia when the Kremlin first invaded Ukraine in 2022, at a cost of $35 billion, as an example of ethical decisions being positive for business.



“It was a big economic decision for them to make, and based on ethical values that they couldn’t remain and be complicit,” Neville said. “If BP were to stay in Russia, it could easily have been that customers elsewhere in the Western, Ukraine-aligned world, could have boycotted BP. It’s the business case of ethics that ultimately drives many of these business decisions, especially in the fossil fuel industry.” He also said that when companies make ethical decisions, it reduced the degree to which government intruded and regulated their industry, benefiting business. Singapore, which recently vowed to keep supplying Australia with fuel, in March increased its imports from Russia by 78 per cent month-on-month. Imports of naphtha, which is used in making jet fuel and fertilisers, hit their highest volume since November 2024. More than half of Australia’s fuel oil imports come from Singapore, followed by South Korea, India, Malaysia and Brunei, according to recent data from the federal energy department.



Australia’s diesel imports are led by South Korea (29 per cent), Singapore (15 per cent), Malaysia (14 per cent), Taiwan (12 per cent) and Brunei (8 per cent). Editor's pick Exclusive

Middle East at war Fuel spike is coming: Relief at bowser not tipped to last When asked about Singapore using Russian oil to replace the shortfall created by the war, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said more oil entering the global market was a good thing. Singaporean companies source oil from all over the world and should respect international sanctions, Wong said, “but subject to that, oil is fungible”. “As long as more oil enters the global energy market, it is good for the world.”



Singapore processes, refines and mixes fuels at its Jurong Island oil hub, which can result in it exporting a “cocktail of product from a couple of different origin and sources [including Russian]“, said Dr Daiyan Rahman, a University of NSW specialist in power fuels. Fuel blended under this process is not considered “transformed” enough to be legal to import. However, the increased amount of Russian fuel products entering Singapore “absolutely” increases the risk that Russian oil could be imported into Australia, said Rahman. Raghunandan said increased trade with Singapore without tightened import parameters would “undoubtedly see a rise in Russian molecules entering Australia”. World.title: AI tool ‘too dangerous to release’ could wreak havoc on businesses
World.content:
TechnologyCybersecurity AI tool ‘too dangerous to release’ could wreak havoc on businesses David Swan May 4, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s largest cybersecurity firm has issued an urgent warning about a powerful new artificial intelligence tool that can find and exploit flaws in software at unprecedented speed and scale, and which experts fear could trigger the next wave of major data breaches. CyberCX on Thursday told Australian businesses, banks and infrastructure operators they had a closing window to shore up their defences before the technology, or copies of it, reach the hands of criminals. Anthropic has plans to broaden bank access to its Mythos cybersecurity tool. Bloomberg The warning deals with Claude Mythos Preview, an unreleased AI model built by US company Anthropic that the firm has deemed too dangerous to release publicly. Anthropic has restricted access to about 50 major technology and infrastructure partners – including Microsoft, Google, Apple, Amazon and JPMorgan Chase – under a program called Project Glasswing. Mythos has already uncovered thousands of previously unknown software flaws, including a 27-year-old bug in an operating system used in firewalls and internet routers worldwide. In one test, it produced 181 working attacks against the Firefox web browser. An earlier, publicly available version managed just two.



Anthropic product lead Angela Jiang said the cyber capability had emerged partly as a by-product of the company’s broader push on coding and long-horizon agentic tasks. “If something’s really good at coding, it’s also very good at detecting cyberattacks, especially over a bunch of different surfaces, and chaining that together,” Jiang said. The company had been “privileged to work with a bunch of companies to help improve critical infrastructure”. Dimitri Vedeneev, secure AI lead at CyberCX, said it was not just Mythos’s ability to find long-buried vulnerabilities that set it apart, but also its capacity to chain multiple flaws together and suggest how to exploit them, all from a single prompt. Anthropic has restricted access to about 50 major technology and infrastructure partners — including Microsoft, Google, Apple, Amazon and JPMorgan Chase - under a program called Project Glasswing. Bloomberg “Australian organisations should not be waiting for access to Mythos as some kind of silver bullet,” Vedeneev said. “It won’t be long until this capability – or others like it – is more widely available, and potentially in the hands of cyber criminals.”



Mythos has rattled governments worldwide. Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey told the BBC central banks were examining what the technology could mean for cybercrime, while Canadian finance minister François-Philippe Champagne described Mythos as an “unknown unknown” at International Monetary Fund meetings in Washington. The Trump administration convened major US bank bosses to discuss the risks. Related Article AI AI giant Anthropic hires Australian boss as it opens local office Anthropic expects competing AI companies to release similarly powerful tools within 18 months. OpenAI has given a select group of users access to its own cyber-focused model, GPT-5.4-Cyber. Bloomberg reported last week that a small group of unauthorised users had obtained access to Mythos through third parties, and Anthropic has confirmed it is investigating. Anthropic on Friday separately announced the public beta launch of Claude Security, a defensive product that allows enterprise customers to scan their own code for vulnerabilities and generate patches. It said hundreds of organisations had used the tool in research previews to find flaws “that existing tools had missed for years.” Accenture, Deloitte, PwC, BCG and Infosys are among those using the product. An Anthropic spokesperson said the company was starting with “some of the largest US-based companies” on the basis that “if they can secure their products quickly, that security extends on a global scale”, adding it looked forward to expanding cybersecurity partnerships.



Not everyone is convinced Mythos represents a clean break. Juraj Janosik, director of AI at cybersecurity firm ESET, said models capable of identifying vulnerabilities had existed well before Mythos. With the right orchestration, threat actors could “already achieve Mythos-like capabilities using generally available models”. “Many companies still lag in maintaining basic cyber hygiene and are often exploited using older, already public vulnerabilities,” Janosik said. “While the developments in AI capability are a concern, they are dwarfed by the overall lack of cyber resilience.” Grattan chief Aruna Sathanapally in discussion with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in Canberra. Manuel Salazar, director of cyber services at Australian firm Orro, said the fundamentals had not changed. “Mythos changes the speed at which weak fundamentals get exposed,” he said. “For mature organisations, AI is a force multiplier; for less mature organisations, it can accelerate uplift, but it cannot bypass the fundamentals.” Salazar said Australian businesses should have access to the defensive benefits of Mythos-class AI but not “unrestricted access to a frontier exploit engine”.



“Australia needs to secure access to advanced AI technologies through agencies like the Australian Signals Directorate, Home Affairs and the National Cyber Security Coordinator,” he said. “If we don’t get involved now, we’re at risk of falling behind our US counterparts.” The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the White House had rejected an Anthropic proposal to roughly double the number of organisations with access to Mythos, citing security concerns. The administration’s relationship with Anthropic has been strained by an earlier dispute over military use of the company’s AI, now the subject of two court cases. It is unclear whether any Australian organisations are part of Project Glasswing. Anthropic signed an agreement with the Albanese government earlier this year and opened a Sydney office, but no Australian agency has publicly confirmed access. The warning lands against the backdrop of the 2022 Optus and Medibank breaches, which combined exposed the personal information of millions of customers and reshaped public trust in major institutions. The breaches exploited comparatively conventional weaknesses, and the fear is that more sophisticated AI tools such as Mythos could allow attackers to find and exploit flaws in systems previously considered secure. CyberCX is urging Australian organisations to map their critical systems, segment their networks and “fight AI with AI” by deploying defensive AI in security functions.
